#782. Fifa to share documents on World Cup sell-off plans with council members

Viewings to take place at Fifa’s headquarters in Zurich

No direct response to Uefa’s questions on governance

Fifa will grant its council members access to documents regarding the doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme but has not responded directly to more than 50 questions from Uefa about its governance and recent scandals.

In a letter sent to the Fifa Council by Mattias Grafström, the governing body’s secretary general, members were told material relating to FFE will be released for them to view in person at Fifa’s headquarters in Zurich. They will be allowed only to view the documents, of which the exact nature and scope are unclear, under strict confidentiality protocols. A deadline of 16 November has been set to apply for such visits; eyebrows may be raised in some quarters about the fact this is two days before candidates for the Fifa election next year are required to declare their hand.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Uefa had written to Grafström on 19 October giving Fifa a fortnight to answer a series of questions about FFE, the Folarin Balogun affair, the Fifa peace prize, the organisation’s relations with Donald Trump and other major decisions that have caused controversy in the past 12 months. It had asked for all documents regarding FFE to be made accessible, saying refusal to comply with any of its demands should be “justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon”.

The deadline imposed by Uefa expired on Monday night, although Fifa Council members are understood to have been told a response is being worked upon and will be shared with them. Fifa’s stance is that Uefa’s questions, posed after Gianni Infantino told delegates at the Fifa Council meeting last month to submit questions in writing before they next convened in December, were too substantial in number for the two-week turnaround.

It remains to be seen whether those Fifa Council members who travel for the document inspection will depart with the answers they require. In August Uefa made an application to four courts in the US for the release of documents pertaining to FFE, with a view to lodging a criminal complaint in Switzerland alleging financial mismanagement. Preliminary rulings are yet to be handed down and the amount of information available to view may be affected. Fifa has accused Uefa of “harassment” and “misinformation” and denied wrongdoing by Infantino.

As reported last week Uefa and its allies are close to identifying a candidate who could stand against Infantino in March, with movement possible early this month.

#781. Newcastle unrest grows as Barry and Everton give Jaissle another headache

Jack Grealish will do well to get back into the Everton starting lineup when he returns to the squad – as David Moyes’s side are doing just fine without him.

Newcastle were condemned to a second defeat in five days by Moyes’s young team, with a second-half goal from Thierno Barry giving Everton victory against 10 men at St James’ Park after the substitute Jacob Ramsey’s late red card.

And there are still more questions than answers about Matthias Jaissle’s new-look side following a summer of transition at the club, and supporters again voiced their disapproval at the end of the game.

Moyes was reluctant to talk about Grealish’s situation, stating simply that the winger was “unavailable” for a second successive game following a breach of club discipline. But, pressed if there was a way back for the winger, he added: “Of course there is.”

Asked about the resilience of his youthful team, Moyes added: “They’re so good, they give everything they’ve got. They’re a brilliant group of players. We beat Newcastle on Thursday night, and to beat them again today, it’s not an easy thing to do for any club.”

Jaissle acknowledged the reaction of Newcastle supporters to the performance and the result. “Big frustration, big disappointment,” he said. “Of course, the fans, they get frustrated like we are. We need to analyse it now in detail. It’s also clear that I have the responsibility, and I also take that as manager of this club. We need to do things better.”

Newcastle fans had made their feelings about the 3-1 Carabao Cup defeat away to Everton last Thursday clear to Jaissle, who has found himself under pressure early in his tenure. By the time he had gone on to the pitch at Hill Dickinson Stadium to acknowledge their backing, most of the 7,732 travelling supporters had headed for the exits, and St James’ Park emptied just as quickly after the home loss.

Eddie Howe was always going to be a hard act to follow given what he achieved in his first four years as head coach at St James’ Park, but the summer departures of big-name players, and his own 11th-hour arrival, has made the job even harder for Jaissle.

Frustration bubbled away beneath the surface at St James’ Park, a stadium which can be a cauldron when fans are given something to shout about. But the decibel levels were rarely raised in the first period. Newcastle’s Harvey Barnes cut inside late in the half, and an awkward deflection off Jarrad Branthwaite momentarily had Jordan Pickford worried, but, in truth, neither he nor Lukas Hornicek in the home goal were troubled in the first 45 minutes. Jake O’Brien and Harrison Armstrong had chances for Everton late in the half, but both shot wide.

Hornicek, however, was finally tested early in the second half – and a mistake from him handed Barry a goal. The goalkeeper let a shot from the left from Tyrique George squirm under his body, and Barry gratefully tapped the ball into an empty net.

Newcastle have given a number of soft goals away this season, and Jaissle conceded that his team had been caught “sleeping” by Everton, who pressed for a second goal before Yoane Wissa and Sean Steur were sent on by Jaissle.

Steur, after a hugely promising start to life at St James’ Park, has found himself on the bench in recent games to the bemusement of some supporters given how well he performed early in the season following his move from Ajax. Soon after Steur’s introduction, Barnes delivered a ball from the left which was met by Anthony Elanga at the back post. The ball rolled along the line, but did not fully cross it, and Everton cleared the danger.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

By now, St James’ Park had livened up, but the home team’s performance still lacked conviction in the final third.

Jaissle sent on Ramsey and Jacob Murphy for the last 15 minutes, but Newcastle found themselves pinned back by Everton, who were a threat on the break.

Half-chances came and went for Newcastle – who did not have a shot on target until the 86th minute, and also had Ramsey sent off for two stoppage-time yellow cards – as the travelling fans made themselves heard high up on Level 7.

The question some Newcastle fans are asking is just how high this team can finish above the Premier League’s relegation zone, as there are still big issues for Jaissle to address at both ends of the pitch ahead of what looks like being a challenging winter.

“The only way is togetherness, showing unity, and then the belief comes,” said Jaissle.

#780. Grealish can still have Everton future - Moyes

Everton hold off Newcastle United to move in to seventh

Everton boss David Moyes says there is a way back for Jack Grealish at the club - but does not know when he will return to the team.

The former England midfielder missed both of the Toffees' wins over Newcastle in the past week after a disciplinary issue.

The 31-year-old Manchester City loanee was left out of Thursday's 3-1 victory in the Carabao Cup - a decision made by the club - after what was thought to be an unauthorised absence from training.

And again on Monday for their Premier League meeting - which Everton won 1-0 at St James' Park with Thierno Barry scoring the only goal - Grealish was absent.

The Toffees said it was because of a lack of fitness - but Moyes was very coy at full-time.

"He's unavailable at the moment and we will make a decision with the club when we think that availability comes back," he told BBC Sport.

When asked whether it was indeed related to fitness, he added: "All I'm giving out is that he is unavailable at the moment."

And when pressed over whether the disciplinary issue is over with, Moyes said: "No, I can't comment on that."

David Moyes post-match interview - Newcastle United v Everton

Everton's next match is at home to Coventry on Friday (20:00 GMT) with Moyes unsure whether Grealish will be available then.

But when asked if there was a way back for him at the club, Moyes said: "Of course there is."

Grealish is trying to rebuild his career at Everton, having fallen out of favour at City despite costing the club Â£100m in 2021.

Grealish, who played a key role helping City win the 2022-23 Treble, will be out of contract at the end of the season.

He scored twice in 22 games for Everton last season during a loan spell which was cut short by injury.

The midfielder returned to the club for a second loan spell this season but had only made six appearances before falling out of favour.

#779. DWTS' Disney Elimination Is Not the Fairest of Them All

Dancing With the Stars bid a fond farewell to one couple on the Nov. 2 Disney Night episode as the duo enjoyed their final magical moment on the dance floor.

Despite a magical evening, one couple had to leave the happiest ballroom floor on Earth during the Nov. 2 Disney Night episode of Dancing With the Stars.

Although they wowed the judges with a Paso Doble set to “Satisfied” from the musical Hamilton, Julia Stiles and her partner Ezra Sosa would no longer be in the room where it happens.

“It's been an incredible experience. I pulled things out of myself that I didn't realize were there,” Stiles said through tears following the elimination. “And Ezra is just an amazing person. I'm going to be sad not to see him every day.”

Sosa was equally downhearted to be saying goodbye, especially because he had seen Stiles grow so much as a dancer throughout the experience.

“Just to see your growth in and outside the ballroom has been an absolute honor,” he told the Save the Last Dance actress. “I'm so lucky that I got to share this experience with you. I love you so much.”

Still, plenty of couples had no worries for the rest of their days during the evening, as Harry Shum Jr. and partner Jenna Johnson received a perfect score for their jazz routine to “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious” from Mary Poppins, as did Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy for their quickstep to “Be Our Guest” from Beauty and the Beast.

Amber Glenn was also ready to shout it from the mountaintops with her partner Pasha Pashkov as the two quickstepped to “A Star Is Born” from Hercules, as Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach let the audience be part of their world, dancing a samba to “Under the Sea” from The Little Mermaid.

Disney’s Broadway adventures also got a moment on the dance floor, as Tatyana Ali and her partner Jan Ravnik took a page from the Broadway book, dancing a contemporary routine to “Easy as Life” from the Disney-produced musical Aida.

Disney Night was certainly a wonderland away from last week’s Horror Movie Night, where the dancers said goodbye to two couples: Savannah Bananas baseball player Jackson Olson and his partner Emma Slater, as well as Bachelor Nation alum Tyler Cameron and pro dancer Sharna Burgess.

And luckily, the dance pros would always have a friend in their partners, with Burgess raving to E! News how close she and Cameron had become outside the ballroom.

"There's been a lot of things happening in my life that he's been an incredible friend through. He's so grounded for his age. He's so well beyond his years that he surprises me sometimes with his wisdom and his depth,” she shared. "I found an amazing human that I just want to keep in my life."

For a look at all the stars hoping to visit a whole new world as the winners of the famed Mirrorball trophy, keep reading.

You won't hate this news—the 10 Things I Hate About You star will be saving the last dance for her pro partner.

The celebrity chef couldn't cha-cha-chop away the competition and was eliminated during the Sept. 22 episode.

What did you miss on Glee? The actor taking his musical talents to the dance floor.

Sadly, the former '90s teen heartthrob did not MMMBop his way to the top of the leaderboard on season 35. He and his pro partner were axed from the competition on Sept. 29.

The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air actress will be bringing her fresh moves to the dance floor.

Twenty years after starring in Step Up, the dancer is stepping up to the challenge.

The 2026 Olympic figure skater will take her skills from the ice to the ballroom.

The Team USA Paralympic track and field athlete will show off his athleticism on DWTS.

Though her sister Brooks Nader was the fifth star to be eliminated on season 33, the Love Thy Nader star said goodbye to the competition after her debut episode on Sept. 16.

The comedian, also known as Fibula on social media, is ready to earn more applause on DWTS.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star followed his wife Whitney Leavitt's footsteps after her season 34 appearance, but he bid farwell to the season 35 competition during the Sept. 15 premiere.

#778. Don’t call it a remontada: Emery’s Camp Nou comeback focuses European blur

The expanded Champions League is often shapeless, but Aston Villa’s manager returning to the scene of his greatest trauma stands out

“One more match. Just one more match.” Sure, Unai. Sure. Just like all the other matches that generated a local tremor measured at 1 on the Richter scale when that seventh and final goal went in at the Camp Nou in March 2017.

It was inevitable that Unai Emery would be asked about the Remontada game on the eve of Aston Villa’s Champions League engagement with Barcelona, his own first trip back to the Camp Nou in this competition since one of the most visceral and traumatic experiences of his managerial career.

Emery was Paris Saint-Germain’s manager the night the Neymar-Messi-Suárez triple-godhead reversed a 4-0 first-leg quarter-final deficit in this stadium.

For all the talk of lasting trauma Emery stayed in Paris for another season, won a domestic treble, and three clubs later has two more European trophies to his name. Plus, of course a trip back here now, with only the lurking shadow of being asked to do the Manchester United job hanging over an otherwise cloudless period in his elite coaching career.

“What happened in that match we know. I started coaching in 2004, 22 years in a row. I’ve played in Europe 16 years in a row. And I’ve learnt in all the competitions and matches. And in that match I learnt so, so much.”

European football has done a pretty good job in the last two seasons of turning its autumn fixture blizzard into a hopeless and baggy blur. What serious sport actually has a 36-team mega table? And a deeply predictable 36-team mega-table at that, one where you pretty much know who’s going to be up there at the end of it. If the intention was to create a series of exhibition-style TV-product events, thereby heading off the Super League’s desire to do exactly the same, then mission semi-accomplished.

There are still exceptions in the period of drift, one-off events that speak to the colour and cultural weight of this competition. Tuesday night is one of them, for Villa’s fans a genuine staging point in the progress of this ever-evolving team, with a chance, dependent on results elsewhere, to actually top the Champions League mega-table at this early stage.

Mainly this feels like a deeply Emery occasion. Not so much a homecoming; the Basque coastal town where he grew up is 350 miles northwest of here. As a player Emery never made it on to the pitch against Barça. But as a manager this has been an endlessly gruelling two-hander: 30 games across Almería, Valencia, Spartak Moscow, Sevilla, PSG and Villarreal, and an ongoing tale of sorrow, with 21 defeats and just three wins.

Not that you’d know it. Emery has always come here with teams that are punching up. He spoke on the eve of his latest return with a genuine conviction about learning from each of those occasions, focused as ever on the possibilities in front of him.

“These games gave me experience to learn, to get better, to intensify for the next matches I face. With the players we talked about our experiences together. We had our experience in Europe, two years ago, last year. This year we have won three matches and done fantastic work. Tomorrow we are facing one of the favourites to win the competition so we are going to face a huge challenge.”

The Camp Nou is still in a state of furious full-body renovation, surrounded by hoardings and railings and rubble-strewn strips of land, but inside the fixings are taking shape. The current team is also a high-functioning work in progress. La Masia continues to produce omni-talented high-technique teenagers. There is a slight, and understandable, sense of a soft centre at times. But also of fluent and dreamy possession football.

Villa will be aggressive, hard-pressing, geared to assert their physical advantages. Their captain, John McGinn, was sat next to his manager in the pop-up press conference room and revealed that he had been here only once before, as an eight-year-old on holiday the same day Ricardo Quaresma signed for Barcelona and had his unveiling at the stadium.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

McGinn talked about his own journey alongside the Villa fans from the Championship to this elite stage. He praised Barcelona’s humility and work ethic. He also said Villa had the players to hurt them.

It is at last a fitting palate cleanser, a chance to move on from the dominant piece of Aston Villa news this so far week, which isn’t actually news or even really anything to do with Aston Villa.

There was a great deal of digital heat over the weekend at Jamie Carragher’s assertion there is “a food chain” in English football, that Aston Villa would naturally remain below Manchester United in this hierarchy, and as such Emery would always feel the need to climb to that higher level.

The only part of this statement that seems unarguably true is that Jamie Carragher doesn’t know how food chains work. In reality a food chain is mutable. This is not a fixed order. Dynamic population. Habitat shifts. Mutable omnivore status. The food chain is constantly rotating, overlapping, redefining itself.

A more accurate analogy would be that the Premier League is unlike a food chain, but is instead a place where money has created genuine stratification. On the other hand, is the thing Jamie Carragher thought he was saying even true?

Villa are pushing hard at the envelope. They’re in Barcelona. They have a proper manager, not Lee Hendrie or similar bringing the emergency DNA. Manchester United is an idea, beloved of legacy consumers, its footprint still vast, but a footprint in sands that are shifting and have shifted and will shift even faster and further.

For Barcelona, Dani Olmo, Andreas Christensen, Eric García and Xavi Espart are expected to miss the game, opening up a little potential defensive frailty. Nicholas Jackson is expected to be fit to start for Villa after playing 90 minutes at the weekend.

#777. Fifa to share 'key documents' over World Cup sell-off plan

Gianni Infantino has been Fifa president since 2016

Fifa says "key documents" relating to president Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors will be made available to members of its council - but access will be subject to "strict review protocols".

Last month, Uefa gave football's world governing body until 2 November to release details about the hugely controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and to answer a list of questions relating to its governance and decision-making.

That followed a council meeting at which Infantino apologised for the abandoned sell-off plot but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised, asking that questions be submitted in writing.

Just hours before the deadline from European football's governing body passed, Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom wrote to members of its main decision-making body - saying they will be able to view "key documents", but only in person at the organisation's headquarters in Zurich.

In his letter - seen by BBC Sport - he says the paperwork will be available "under strict review protocols to preserve confidentiality", with council members asked to register to see them within the next two weeks.

It is unclear which documents will be made available.

BBC Sport has been told Fifa viewed Uefa's two-week deadline to respond to more than 100 questions as unfeasible, given their recent focus on organising a new youth World Cup in Azerbaijan and preparations for an extraordinary congress later this month.

Sources have also indicated Fifa's ability to answer some questions is limited by legal action that Uefa launched in October in the US, requesting disclosure of evidence and documents, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.

Last month, Uefa told Fifa that it had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions".

The letter included eight pages of questions covering a number of issues, from FFE and funding to national associations, to the awarding of an inaugural Fifa Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump and the controversial suspended ban given to USA striker Folarin Balogun at the World Cup.

"The withdrawal of FFE, the acknowledgement of mistakes and the announcement of 'potential governance reforms' do not answer how the relevant decisions were taken or why the Fifa Council was not involved at the appropriate stage," the letter said.

"These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the Fifa Council - nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them."

Uefa did not outline what steps it intended to take should Fifa not meet the deadline, but hoped it added to the pressure on Infantino before 18 November - the cut-off date for any candidates to confirm they are standing against him in next year's presidential election.

In his letter Grafstrom says that Uefa's demand "contains significantly more questions than the Fifa administration could reasonably have anticipated" and that it is "currently working on a response which we will share with all council members in due course."

He adds that the FFE proposal "could not have proceeded without the cumulative and mandatory approval of the council, and a majority of member associations, and in that event, there would be and has been no penalty to Fifa for withdrawing from the proposal".

#776. Carrick says it's 'crazy' but he's looking forward to Roma game

Michael Carrick signed a two-year contract in the summer

Michael Carrick accepts it might sound "crazy" but the beleaguered Manchester United boss says he is looking forward to the Champions League showdown with Roma at Old Trafford.

United go into Tuesday's game without a win in nine matches in all competitions.

It is their worst run since 1988-89. They have not gone 10 without a win in a single campaign since 1977-78 and there is a growing feeling Carrick will lose his job during the forthcoming international break.

Roma's only defeat so far this season was at home to Real Madrid in the Champions League last month, when they led 3-1 with seven minutes left.

United are 17th in the Premier League and after defeats by Atletico Madrid and Como have slumped to 21st in the Champions League table after three games, with only the top 24 making it through.

It is a bleak backdrop, but rather than fret over what lies ahead, Carrick is viewing it as a chance to change the narrative of the season.

"You might think I'm crazy with the results we've had and what's going on, but genuinely, I really can't wait for the game," said Carrick. "I'm really looking forward to it.

"Listen, I can't look into the future, you never know what's going to happen. That doesn't change the way I feel. Whatever happens is going to happen in whatever direction it goes in, but we want to make it a big night tomorrow."

Carrick watched over a lively open session of pre-match training at Carrington.

Striker Bryan Mbeumo and midfielder Carlos Baleba were particularly vocal, with Argentina defender Lisandro Martinez also fully engaged despite his red card at Chelsea, which triggered such a negative reaction.

While there have been calls for Martinez to be dropped for the Roma game, Carrick was more philosophical.

"Sometimes you do things; you make a decision, you make mistakes. Sometimes it goes well for you."

He also dismissed concerns both about Martinez's commitment, and that of his entire squad.

"Perceptions are a funny thing," he said.

"They can make things look all sorts of different ways. The dressing room is a good place.

"I've said it before, I don't question the commitment of the players, to the club and to me and to each other. We need to play better. We can make better decisions. But commitment's not a thing at all."

'You might think I'm crazy' - Carrick excited for Roma game despite struggles

England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo sat alongside Carrick at the media conference and also stressed the strength of the group.

Mainoo returned from a four-match absence with a muscular issue as a second-half substitute at Chelsea.

At 21, Mainoo is one of the youngest players in Carrick's squad. However, given he joined the club as a seven-year-old, he is also the longest serving and has a unique insight into the responsibilities that come with life in the Old Trafford spotlight.

"I've been at this club for a long time and know there's always going to be ups and downs," he said. "It's never going to be plain sailing and smooth to the top. You expect bumps.

"Of course it's been a tough season. We've not had the results we've wanted, but I feel like we're one win away from changing that."

United were last relegated in 1973-74. They have not been in the relegation zone after nine games or more since November 1986, when they collected a single point in Sir Alex Ferguson's first two games in charge following Ron Atkinson's dismissal.

Their lowest position after at least nine games of a season since then was 17th in 1989-90. They were 16th under Ruben Amorim after 37 games of the 2024-25 season.

Mainoo says the present position is unacceptable for a club of United's size.

"United's a huge club," he said. "I think a lot of people know the values this club holds and have been passed down through the people who've worked here and played here.

"I feel like I take some responsibility in spreading the word of what Manchester United is, coming up through the academy, and I plan to send that message for as long as I can."

#775. Ariana Grande & Ricky Álvarez Write Note to Stranger at NYC Marathon

Ariana Grande and her boyfriend Ricky Álvarez were spotted in the crowd at the New York City Marathon, cheering on runners as they made it to the finish-line.

Ariana Grande put a spring in the step of one lucky marathon runner.

The “Into You” singer and boyfriend Ricky Álvarez helped influencer Ella Schweiger create a random act of kindness during the New York City Marathon Nov. 1, writing an encouraging note for Schweiger to share with a runner after the race.

In a video posted to Instagram Nov. 2, Schweiger could be seen approaching Álvarez and Grande as they watched the marathon from the crowd, asking if they wouldn’t mind writing the note. And Grande—who was dressed incognito with a face mask—was more than happy to make sure someone had a message after the final stretch. On her notecard, the 33-year-old drew three hearts and wrote, “You did it, Ari + Ricky.”

Following the marathon, Schweiger had runners pick out a note from her trademark giant envelope and was delighted when someone nabbed Grande’s message.

“I can’t believe you picked that one. That’s from Ariana Grande,” she shared with the lucky recipient. “She wrote that this morning."

And the marathoner was beside herself with shock, revealing that she was even listening to Grande’s “The Way” to help her go the distance.

Schweiger also expressed her gratitude in her Instagram caption, saying, “It was so lovely of her to take the time to write a message for a complete stranger who just did one of the toughest challenges in the world!”

“Then getting to deliver it to the most amazing girl and see her reaction was just was incredible,” she continued. “Ariana, thank you for being part of it and to everyone who wrote a message, you made someone’s day.”

The day after Grande and Álvarez enjoyed their private date out in NYC, the “7 Rings” singer gave a more public glimpse into their romance in a Nov. 2 Instagram carousel, posting a photo of the two embracing as they made intimate eye contact with each other.

Grande and Álvarez first dated from 2015 to 2016, but rekindled their romance earlier this year following her split from Wicked costar Ethan Slater.

The Grammy winner also shared a special message to Álvarez while on tour, proving he could be her finish-line, as she changed the lyrics of her song "thank u, next" from, "Wrote some songs about Ricky / Now I listen and laugh," to, ”Wrote some songs about Ricky / I’m tryna make him my last.”

For a look at more stars who helped put their mark on marathons, keep reading.

The singer was heading in one direction—towards the finish line—at both the 2025 Tokyo Marathon and Berlin Marathon.

"NYC Marathon, round 2!!" the former Bachelorette wrote on Instagram ahead of the 2024 race after having run it three years prior with her former fiancé Zac Clark. "Bib #38793 in hand and ready for the big day! Can’t wait to see you all cheering out there — I’ll need every bit of that energy!"

After finishing the 2024 Chicago Marathon, The Originals star reflected on her journey."I think one of the most important traits in life is humility, but I’m going to let myself feel proud," she wrote on Instagram. "I woke up at 4am all summer to train for this race. It was really f*cking hard and I asked a lot of my family during those 4 months."

"I doubted myself more often than not, and I was sick to my stomach at the thought of letting anyone down," Holt added. "But today I ran a personal best by 19 minutes (3:44:14), 11 months after having my 3rd kid. I did it because of the unbelievable generosity of friends, family and kind-hearted strangers. I did it because you believed in me, and the cause. Together we raised over $100,000 to help Boston Children’s Hospital tackle the mental health crisis. I am so beyond grateful to you all. Thank you, from the bottom of my heart."

The Banshees of Inisherin star ran the 2024 Irish Life Dublin Marathon.

The Amy & T.J. podcast hosts flashed their medals after finishing the 2023 New York City Marathon.

"So I did a thing….26.2miles of a thing…. In 3hrs35 minutes," the Wicked star shared on Instagram after finishing the 2022 London Marathon. "I’m proud and I’m exhausted and I’m grateful!! X. @londonmarathon was emotional."

Hello Wisconsin, er, New York! The That '70s Show alum celebrated after finishing the NYC Marathon in 2022.

The Sunday Today host helped raise more than $400,000 for the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Disease while participating in the 2021 New York City Marathon.

The Bachelor Nation stars posed for a pic at the finish line of the New York City Marathon with Matt's now-ex Rachael Kirkconnell in 2021.

We're not catfishing you. The Catfish host has run several marathons, including the 2019 New York City Marathon.

Though the former Bachelorette told People her goal was simply to finish the hilly 26.2-mile course in New York City ("I don't want to be disappointed," she explained of getting her heart set on a specific time) the reality star walked away from the 2019 event with an impressive sub-four-hour finish time.

A year after he tackled his first marathon in NYC, the comedian participated in the 2018 Chicago Marathon to raise funds to help send kids to college. "The reason behind this run is simply first and foremost personal greatness, personal achievement but also what I can bring awareness to, what I can raise money for," he shared on Instagram, shouting, "Education!"

For the model, the 2017 New York City Marathon was, "Singlehandedly the hardest thing I've ever done." Still, she crushed the course in four hours, 41 minutes.

"One foot in front of the other was my mantra," Alicia posted about finishing the 2015 marathon in the concrete jungle where dreams are made of. (She notched a time of 5:50:52.) And for the Grammy winner, the race was an energizing challenge. "I'm all about breaking mental boundaries," she wrote in a Refinery29 blog post, "and training for a marathon falls right into the Jedi mind-training I need."

Though the Game of Thrones star insisted she didn't care much about her time in the 2016 London Marathon—noting raising upwards of $7,000 for The National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children's ChildLine service was more important—she admitted to reporters she was "a tiny bit peeved," about her three-hour, 54-minute finish considering it was 24 seconds slower than her 2014 debut.

Running the Boston Marathon in 2015 for the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, the Orange Is the New Black star listened to Sara Bareilles' "Brave" in tribute to a friend she lost to the disease. "That was her motivator getting through every single day of treatment, every single round of chemo, that was what she was listening to constantly," she explained. "And I listen to that when I'm training now, and I can hear her telling me, 'Keep going.'"

Seeing his dad battle Parkinson's disease inspired the Deadpool actor to run the New York City Marathon in 2008. Finishing in three hours, 50 minutes, he also raised money to help fight the disease by teaming up with Michael J. Fox's Team Fox.

After finishing the NYC marathon in 2007, the actress turned up (in heels!) alongside then-husband Tom Cruise for his Lions for Lambs premiere.

"Running a marathon is not a question of whether it will be painful, but when it will be painful," the actor said after finishing his third marathon—Boston's 2003 race—in less than four hours. He later noted to Podium Runner that people "are terribly underwhelmed when they recognize me in a race. There's nothing funny going on. It's just a lot of silence and pain."

After vowing to take on a marathon before she turned 40, the queen of daytime television ran 26.2 miles in Washington, D.C. in 1994. In the pouring rain. As two National Enquirer reporters tagged along tracking her every move. She finished in an impressive four hours, 29 minutes.

Having kept up with the sport long after he ran the Houston course in 1993, Bush accepted few excuses from people who said they simply couldn't squeeze a workout in.

"I believe anyone can make the time [to run]," he told Runner's World during his term. "As a matter of fact, I don't believe it—I know it. If the President of the United States can make the time, anyone can."

#774. Germany sit out FIFA Under-15 World Cup as Russia return

Germany is one a handful of FIFA's 211 nations to refuse an invitation to play at the inaugural Under-15 World Cup. The tournament will also mark Russia's return to the FIFA fold.

With nearly 1,000 matches and 189 teams, the Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan is bloated even by FIFA's usual standards. It marks a change in its attitude to children's international tournaments, which have not existed on anywhere near this scale before.

For Germany, it is too much too soon. The German FA (DFB) told DW that it had "consciously decided not to participate." The statement from the organization suggested the DFB — whose development of young players is under scrutiny after a run of poor performances by the men's national team — felt such a tournament was not appropriate for players so young.

"At this age level, our identification and development process is still underway, and we therefore do not believe it is appropriate to nominate a fixed squad for an international tournament at this stage," it read.

"More broadly, the DFB's approach to talent development is based on the principle of supporting young players in a long-term and age-appropriate manner. We carefully assess at which stage international competitions and development measures are beneficial for each age group.

"In our view, young talents should not be exposed too early to the accompanying aspects of professional football. These include increased expectations and pressure, public evaluation of their performances, and early interest from agents and the football market."

The refusal to play in the tournament, which began this week, is consistent with Germany's more cautious approach to youth development. While in some leagues, like the Premier League in England, there is no regulation about youths playing professionally, in Germany's top flight, the Bundesliga, players must be 16. In fact, before the 2020-21 season, players could not be granted a pro license before they were 17 years and six months old.

That change enabled Youssoufa Moukoko to make his Bundesliga debut for Borussia Dortmund a day after his 16th birthday in 2020, becoming the league's youngest player in the process.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But, some would argue his is a cautionary tale. Hyped wildly due to his goalscoring exploits at youth level, Moukoko was fast-tracked by Dortmund and Germany, who called him up for the 2022 World Cup. Now, still just 21, he is struggling for game time and goals on loan at Corum, in the Turkish Super League, from Danish side Copenhagen.

Players under 16 are also forbidden by FIFA from having an agent. But this is poorly regulated in some regions of the world. That led Bundesliga club St. Pauli, then in the second division, to announce they would no longer work with player agents or private agencies in their youth system in 2023.

"We want to focus on partnership and dialogue with the players, their families and their relatives," explained the head of the club's youth academy, Benjamin Liedtke, as St. Pauli officially positioned themselves "against the commercialization of youth football."

Germany are one of 22 nations to refuse the invitation to compete in the tournament, 18 of whom are from UEFA, Europe's confederation. The USA are also one of the prominent refusals alongside Ukraine, whose FA told German public broadcaster Sportschau that they initially refused on sporting grounds before claiming that "other countries indicated that they would compete but did not want to play against Russia." DW contacted a number of FAs to clarify this point but is yet to receive a response.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who has become a notorious figure thanks to a number of scandals over the past year, told Sky in February: "We have to [look at reinstating Russia], definitely, because this ban has not achieved anything. It has just created frustration and hatred. Having girls and boys from Russia being able to play football games in other parts of Europe would help."

Eight months later, he has his wish. The ongoing tournament, billed as the "FIFA U-15 World Cup & Festival" comprises eight-a-side games with 20 minute halves, a smaller pitch and a number of other technical tweaks. FIFA say the 2027 edition will be for girls teams only.

"Young players need meaningful matches, different opponents and different football experiences in order to develop. Talent exists everywhere, but the opportunities available to young players are not always the same," said FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger, likely referencing that teams from Bhutan and Seychelles to the Bahamas and Vanuatu are present.

"This tournament gives players from across the world the chance to compete, to learn and to grow."

FIFA are yet to respond to a DW request for further comment.

The round robin stage, according to FIFA, has placed teams in "groups that provide diverse sporting and regional representation" but also appears to have, at least initially, kept apart nations in conflict with each other.

For example, Israel and Palestine or Kosovo and Serbia are not in the same groups but could, in theory, meet in the later stages of the tournament. This would not be allowed in senior football, thanks to various bans and workarounds.

FIFA are vague about how the tournament works after the round robin, saying only that it will consist of "four to five additional matches per team, determined by results and subsequent tier placement. [There will be] one winner for each of the six tiers." It also said that the winner of the top tier will be crowned champions but all teams will play matches until the tournament concludes on October 30.

But, given that they have been banned from international football since invading Ukraine in 2022, it is the presence of a Russian national team at a FIFA tournament that will likely heap the most controversy on to young shoulders. Though a Russian presence was not the reason for German refusal, not attending for sporting reasons may also turn out to be a smart piece of sport politics.

#773. Emery looks to show Villa can compete with elite

Unai Emery has marked four years at Aston Villa after replacing Steven Gerrard

Unai Emery walked into Villa Park four years ago with two clear aims.

"My dream is to win a trophy with Aston Villa. It's my challenge," he said at his unveiling in November 2022.

"My second dream and my objective could be to play with Aston Villa in Europe. But now, we have to start thinking only the next match because we are not in good position in the table now."

Fast-forward to today and Villa will run out at the Nou Camp to face Barcelona in the Champions League on Tuesday night, having won the Europa League in May and with it ending a 30-year trophy drought.

Emery has already achieved his goals, which has led to natural speculation about the next step - with Villa or elsewhere.

Villa were angered to the point of threatening legal action when Sky Sports pundit Jamie Carragher said Emery would want to manage an elite club, with Manchester United admirers.

Villa, though, see themselves as a club ready to join the elite - having challenged them in the Premier League and Europe for the past two years - with Emery leading the way.

Emery celebrates his 55th birthday on Tuesday by facing Barca back in his home country.

Carragher's assertion the Spaniard would be open to leaving Villa was naive, given how much Emery controls matters at the club and the success he has had with them, even if it was not the most sensational of opinions.

He signed his most recent contract in May 2024, taking him to 2029, so Villa are protected - but there will ultimately be a new deal following the Europa League triumph.

He has taken Villa up the pecking order, but they are still not at the top of it - though they remain well placed, as the signing of Johan Manzambi from Freiburg showed.

Villa still lost players in the summer to traditionally bigger clubs: Emi Martinez, Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, with Ollie Watkins also leaving for Saudi Arabia. But the changes have given Emery new vigour.

Nights at the Nou Camp give the Spaniard the chance to prove his worth and the progress made at Villa.

"We are constantly seeking new challenges and we want to respond in games against Barcelona to see how far we are from them," he said.

"We won it [the European Cup] in 1982 and right now we are enjoying reminiscing with our fans, playing in this competition again, and trying to repeat that success.

"Barca are favourites because of the present and what they have done over the last 10 years, but they need to confirm their favourite role.

"The way this league stage goes, to end up finishing it in the first eight we need to avoid any kind of surprise.

"There will be times during the season when you walk your own path, but it needs to be clear the second part of the season is when things will be decided.

"Barcelona have six points, we have nine. We need to find out our personality and make the most of our qualities."

Emery was handed carte blanche to change Villa when he was appointed as Steven Gerrard's successor, and he has transformed them from Premier League strugglers to Europa League winners and Champions League challengers.

His methods are intense - players can have several long meetings during the week and can take months to adapt to his demands.

For instance, internally, there is an acceptance it is why Aaron Wan-Bissaka has struggled so far this season, having not had the same level of coaching at West Ham.

The exhaustive nature of his character played a part in former president of football operations Monchi leaving last year, with Emery's close confidante needing a break.

But that meticulousness is also what makes Emery and his teams so effective.

Barcelona sources fear Villa and Emery, citing the struggles of Alejandro Balde and Joao Cancelo's lack of defensive instinct at how Villa can exploit them, given Emery's capacity to plan and pounce on an opponent's weakness.

Barcelona manager Hansi Flick has won successive La Liga titles with the club

Emery has earned admirers, including Barcelona boss Hansi Flick, following his achievements at Villa, having already won the Europa League three times with Sevilla and once with Villarreal.

"He is one of the best coaches in Europe and the world. He is very successful," Flick said. "In the way his team plays, you can see a clear structure, and in offence they have different patterns. For me, it is amazing to see his team.

"The start was not easy, but they came back. You can see the confidence they have on the ball, how they play out, and Jackson is at an unbelievable level. For us, it will be a tough game against a good team and, as well, a great coach."

Barca winger Anthony Gordon also called him "one of the best in the world" before the game, even though Emery's record at the Nou Camp is wretched.

He has lost 14 of his 15 games there, having only beaten Barcelona three times in 30 attempts. His last Champions League game at the stadium was Paris St-Germain's collapse as they lost 6-1 in the last 16, having won the first leg 4-0.

It is a record Emery is eager to change to further cement his status and reputation.

"Everything happened in that match, we know," he said, with no English team winning at the Nou Camp since Liverpool in 2007.

"I started in 2004, playing in Europe 16 years in a row, different competitions, I have learned in all the competitions. In that match I learned so much. The necessity of VAR for football in that moment.

"In my experiences they [his games at the Nou Camp] were giving me a lot of info to learn and get better.

"With the players we are speaking about our experiences together, we have our experience in Europe, in the Champions League two years ago.

"We are facing one of the favourite teams to win the competition, it is a huge challenge. We are confident how we are building the team, how we are facing teams like Barcelona .

"We are here progressing, understanding, setting our demands and competing the level we are, this is the challenge we have."

#772. See Will Smith Reunite With Ex-Wife Sheree Zampino on Australia Trip

Will Smith and ex-wife Sheree Zampino—with whom he welcomed son Trey before having kids Jaden and Willow with wife Jada Pinkett Smith—spent time in Australia after wrapping his movie Supermax.

Will Smith's pursuit of happiness took him Down Under with Sheree Zampino.

The Oscar winner was a long way from West Philadelphia when he shared a few laughs with his ex-wife—mom to their 33-year-old son Trey Smith—during the tail end of a trip to Australia.

The former couple, who were married from 1992 to 1995, were all smiles as they stepped into the Sydney airport Oct. 28. Smith's time in the Emerald City came to an end following the shoot for his upcoming action movie Supermax, a murder mystery that takes place inside the world's most secure prison.

As such, it's no surprise the I Am Legend star opted for comfort on his travel day, rocking a plush blue hoodie and cozy sweatpants. For her part, the RHOBH alum mixed casual and couture, pairing a Maison Goyard tote with her all-black outfit and matching sandals.

And as Will—also dad to Jaden, 28, and Willow, 25, with wife Jada Pinkett Smith—and Sheree have stayed close as co-parents over the years, the beauty entrepreneur has also forged a bond with the Set It Off actress.

"Coming into this, doing the blended thing, my only requirement was that you treated my son well," Sheree, 58, said during a 2022 episode of Jada’s Red Table Talk. "You did that. And your heart was always right towards him, wanting the best for him."

But that doesn't mean their relationship went off without a hitch. As Jada put it, it did take her some time to understand Sheree and Will's co-parenting dynamic.

"For me, it really was just about maturity," the 55-year-old said. "Not understanding the marital dynamic. Like, ‘OK, if divorce papers are sent and people are over it, then this is done.' Guess what? It ain't never done.”

She added, "So, that was my biggest misconception."

Jada—who is still legally married to Will but shared in 2023 that they’d been separated for years—also confessed there was a time when overstepping with her stepson, Trey, made a tough dynamic worse.

"I can remember some times that I really crossed the line," she admitted in 2022. "It was a lot of intertwining, and it got kind of messy."

But with learning to respect each other's boundaries over time, a family foundation formed out of the tension. As the Matrix alum put it, "We were able to have difficult conversations, we were able to own up."

And throughout their decades together, Will and Jada have stayed candid about their romance. The most legendary quotes about their marriage await...

"We don't even say we're married anymore. We refer to ourselves as 'life partners,' where you get into that space where you realize you are literally with somebody for the rest of your life," Will Smith said during an interview with TIDAL's Rap Radar podcast. "There's no deal breakers. There's nothing she could do—ever—nothing that would break our relationship. She has my support till death, and it feels so good to get to that space."

"I've heard all the things—their marriage is not real, he's gay, she's gay, they swing. But at the end of the day, people have to believe what they have to believe. I'll tell you what, it's too hard to be in a pretend marriage. Life's too short for that one." — Jada Pinkett Smith on Atlanta's Q100

"There's really not a secret per se. If you don't get divorced that year, you get to add one more year to your marriage." — Will Smith to E! News

"Should we be married to individuals who can not be responsible for themselves and their families within their freedom? Should we be in relationships with individuals who we can not entrust to their own values, integrity, and LOVE...for us??? Here is how I will change my statement...Will and I BOTH can do WHATEVER we want, because we TRUST each other to do so. This does NOT mean we have an open relationship...this means we have a GROWN one." — Jada Pinkett Smith on Facebook.

"I'm not gonna be silly. I'm here to honor you. Just watching the piece with the kids it just takes me back to when we made them. Can't help but think about that. It's just amazing. It's like you take Jada Pinkett Smith and an obscure town in Mexico and some tequila and you end up with great kids!" — Will Smith at Vh1's Dear Mama Event

"You gotta trust who you're with, and at the end of the day, I'm not here to be anybody's watcher. I'm not his watcher. He's a grown man. I trust that the man that Will is is a man of integrity. HE's got all the freedom in the world, and as long as Will can look at himself in the mirror and be OK, I'm good." —Jada Pinkett Smith on The Howard Stern Show

"In the interest of redundant, repetitious, over & over-again-ness... Jada and I are...NOT GETTING A DIVORCE!!!!!!!!!!!!! : -) I promise you all - if I ever decide to divorce my Queen - I SWEAR I'll tell you myself! #‎Dumb‬ People Should Have to Wear Scarlet D's." — Will Smith on Facebook

"I never thought about being married or having a family. I didn't know anything about that because I came from a single mom so I always though I'd be a single mom and have a career. Then I found this beautiful man, Will. I got married to him and I got my bonus son Trey and then I got Jaden and I got Willow and I was able to create, for myself, something I never had—which means family." — Jada Pinkett Smith at Vh1's Dear Mama Event

"She is just absolutely hardcore, like she absolutely is unfazed by the weight and the pressures of life. She is so calm and cool and easy in any situation. She can bear anything, and I just love that about her." — Will Smith to People

"If you really want to know, I'm thankful for the Hollywood scrutiny, that that's my problem. There are mothers out there losing their sons, their husbands, their daughters. I'm blessed. So scrutinize me. I'll take that any day over what the majority of my people are dealing with on a daily basis. I dare not complain." — Jada Pinkett Smith to American Way magazine

"He's been by my side through some of the most difficult parts of my life. And so that's something you can never take away. A lot of other things, you never know, other things might change...but one thing is for sure: I love him deeply and he is my best friend." — Jada Pinkett Smith on HuffPost Live

#771. Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?

After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Bart Verbruggen (Brighton): He was unreal. Lots of saves which kept Brighton in it at Manchester City, even the last-ditch stop where it hit him in the face.

Just an impenetrable wall. Brighton should really have lost by two or three goals, but Verbruggen was the reason they managed to hold on for a 1-0 win.

Archie Gray (Tottenham): I'm going with a fully north London back four. Gray scored and defended really well against Crystal Palace. He was under a lot of pressure when Tottenham were in bad form and got a lot of stick, but now Spurs are starting to pick up I'm going to give him a bit of credit.

Ezri Konsa (Arsenal): He was a beast in Arsenal's 1-0 win at Anfield. Head it, kick it, throw your body in front of the ball. He defended and fought for the team, getting the job done.

Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham): Van Hecke got a goal and he's really growing into his role at Spurs. I still think he was a little bit overpriced, but all in all he's had a solid start, coming up with a few goals. Micky van de Ven next to him gives him confidence that he can go and be really aggressive, because Van der Ven will cover him with his pace.

Jurrien Timber (Arsenal): Timber got away with a shirt pull on Alexander Isak and I'm really surprised the referee and video assistant referee (VAR) didn't look at it. But I thought he recovered and defended really well at full-back.

Romeo Lavia (Chelsea): I thought Lavia was excellent for Chelsea. People will turn to Manchester United having 10 men, but the 60 minutes before that Chelsea were all over the place. Lavia was the only constant breaking up play, keeping the ball moving. Plus he had an assist.

Declan Rice (Arsenal): A proper captain's performance, he gets the job done all over the pitch. He got a little assist for himself, too.

Tatsuhiro Sakamoto (Coventry): Sakamoto goes unnoticed by a lot of people, but I think he works really hard for the team and he is very humble in his approach. On Saturday he also delivered in a massive win for his team against Sunderland.

Johan Manzambi (Aston Villa): Another assist for the 21-year-old who is just flying. His confidence is through the roof and he is taking over this Villa team. Really good player, only going to get better. He was taken off thinking about the Champions League game against Barcelona, but up until that point Fulham couldn't really stop him.

Ollie McBurnie (Hull): Grafter, scrappy, endeavour, goals, assists... he had it all in his game in the draw against Ipswich.

He epitomises what Hull are: a player that's always overlooked, a team that's always overlooked, but they've got some spirit and some fight.

Taiwo Awoniyi (Coventry): Unbelievable solo goal. It's really good to see the big fella back playing and being in a situation where he can impose himself. If Coventry are to stay up, he's going to be why.

Frank Lampard (Coventry): He has been really good. Coventry have taken care of business against Sunderland, it was a massive six-pointer and his team came out front-footed, aggressive and also did a job on a very good Sunderland team.

Also a massive nod to Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta for getting the job done at Liverpool.

#770. Who produced the kind of performance Moyes loves? - player ratings

Everton hold off Newcastle United to move in to seventh

A goalkeeping howler by Lukas Hornicek gifted Everton their first Premier League away win since February as 10-man Newcastle United slumped to a fourth defeat in six top-flight games.

Here's how I rated the Newcastle and Everton players, and you can see how you scored them below.

Grealish can still have Everton future - Moyes

Premier League: Everton beat disappointing Newcastle as Ramsey sees late red - reaction

Lukas Hornicek: Horrible mistake to allow Tyrique George's routine attempt to squirm under his body and present Thierno Barry with the goal. 4

Amar Dedic: A passing accuracy of 59.1% in the opening 70 minutes says it all. 4

Fabian Schar: Got forward and had three attempts but unable to help his side to a clean sheet. 5

Dan Burn: The Newcastle captain was booked for a foul on Barry right on the edge of the box. Fortunately for Burn, the set-piece came to nothing. 6

Lewis Hall: The kind of tidy performance we have come to expect from the England player. 7

Nico Gonzalez: Substituted as Newcastle slipped to an alarming fourth defeat in six Premier League games. 5

Joelinton: Produced one clever shot on the turn which looked to be heading for the net before James Tarkowski got in the way. Went close with another from distance. 6

Anthony Elanga: Came close to equalising when he kneed the ball on to the post before Everton just about got it clear. 5

Joe Willock: Replaced by Yoane Wissa. A long way short of his finest form. 5

Harvey Barnes: Lively start and the former Leicester winger went close to marking his 100th Premier League appearance for Newcastle with the 100th goal of his career. 6

William Osula: Was doubtful after twisting his ankle at Everton last week. Started but just seven touches in the first half. 5

Yoane Wissa (on 64, Joe Willock): Unable to find an equaliser. 4

Sean Steur (on 64, Nico Gonzalez): Could not influence the game. 4

Jacob Ramsey (on 75, Joelinton): Sent on to rescue the game. Got sent off. 3

Jacob Murphy (on 75, Anthony Elanga) Little impact. 3

Bazoumana Toure (on 87, Amar Dedi) Seven touches, three passes. 4

Subs not used: Nick Pope, Sven Botman, Aladji Bamba, Malick Thiaw.

Jordan Pickford: The former Sunderland keeper was predictable on the receiving end of relentless stick from the home fans but had the last laugh. 7

Jake O'Brien: Helped his side to a third straight Premier League win at St James' Park as the Toffees registered their fourth top-flight clean sheet of the season. 7

James Tarkowski: A commanding captain's performance as Everton won a Premier League away game for the first time since February. 7

Jarrad Branthwaite: Made a winning return to the side after missing the previous two matches because of concussion protocols. 7

Vitalii Mykolenko: Neat and tidy. Worked hard as the Toffees catapulted up the table from 14th to 7th. 7

Merlin Rohl: The German provided energy, got himself into some dangerous positions and went close with one attempt in the first half which cleared the bar. 7

Harrison Armstrong: Covered his face with his shirt after missing a great chance to put his side ahead on the stroke of half-time. 7

James Garner: A gritty performance, the type which David Moyes loves. Played his part in a fine away win. 8

Tyrique George: Heavily involved in the goal. It was his shot that led to the mistake that saw Everton take the lead. 7

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall: Got stuck in and had an effort tipped over the bar. 7

Thierno Barry: Cannot stop scoring. Although this was the easiest goal he will ever score in his life after a goalkeeping howler. 7

Brennan Johnson (on 80, Thierno Barry): Helped his side get over the line. 5

Michael Keane (on 82, Jarrad Branthwaite): Helped Everton to clean sheet win. 5

Hayden Hackney (on 92, Tyrique George): Five touches, three passes. 4

Subs not used: Ainsley Maitland-Niles, Mark Travers, Tyler Dibling, Christian Norgaard, Charly Alcaraz, Braiden Graham.

#769. Bruce Springsteen Backs Michigan’s Dr. Abdul El-Sayed for U.S. Senate Amid Haley Stevens Reversal: ‘He’s a Fighter’

"I'm in his corner 100%," the Boss said of the Democratic nominee.

Bruce Springsteen has shared his thoughts on the race in Michigan for U.S. Senate, backing Dr. Abdul El-Sayed for the seat as Election Day draws nearer.

In a Monday (Nov. 2) post on Instagram, The Boss shared a statement explaining why he supports the Democratic nominee. “Dr. El-Sayed is a fighter for our American Constitution,” Springsteen wrote. “He’s a fighter for our American Democracy, and he’s a fighter against the corrupt, lawless, and anti-American leadership currently in the White House.”

The musician added, “I’m in his corner 100%.”

The endorsement comes amid a close race in Michigan between Dr. El-Sayed and his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, to take over Democrat Gary Peters’ seat in the Senate. A Democratic win in Michigan is crucial for Democrats as they work to flip the Senate, and recently, Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens threw everyone a curveball by rescinding her support of Dr. El-Sayed and endorsing Rogers. As a result, the state’s Democratic Party chairman Curtis Hertel announced on X that Stevens “is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”

Springsteen has long been vocal in his political opinions, especially in recent years. He’s repeatedly spoken out against Donald Trump in particular, which has led the president to publicly take aim at the Rock & Roll Hall of Famer a number of times — not that it’s had any success in silencing the Boss.

“I do what I want to do,” Springsteen — who’s topped the Billboard 200 11 times over the course of his career — told Rolling Stone of using his recent Land of Hopes & Dreams trek as a political statement. “This was the show I wanted to make, the story I wanted to tell … I’m sure there were people, and I’ve read things where people were vehement about the content of the show. And that’s just the way the chips fall.”

See Springsteen’s endorsement of Dr. El-Sayed below.

#768. Meet Neuropixels: how probes that track hundreds of brain cells at once are revolutionizing neuroscience

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Diana Kwon is a science writer in Berlin.

Neuropixels probes are designed to record the electrical activity of hundreds of neurons at once. Credit: Allen Institute

In a bright surgical theatre in central London, neurosurgeon Ahmed Toma makes an incision on the side of a woman’s head. Then, he bores a small hole into her skull, revealing a glimpse of the pink, pulsating brain beneath.

Even the unconscious brain can learn — and predict what you’ll say next

Even the unconscious brain can learn — and predict what you’ll say next

Toma is preparing to implant a shunt to drain excess cerebrospinal fluid — a routine treatment for a condition called normal pressure hydrocephalus, in which fluid builds up inside the skull. His patient at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery (NHNN) has also agreed to take part in an experiment: one that involves briefly placing a centimetre-long probe, thinner than a human hair, into her brain. Called Neuropixels, this probe is designed to record the electrical activity of hundreds of neurons at once.

As Toma and a team of researchers carefully insert the probe into the patient’s brain, Mihaly Kollo, a research scientist at the Francis Crick Institute in London, stands nearby, monitoring a multicoloured array of outputs from the probe’s recording sites in real time. After controlling for electrical noise from the operating table and other surgical equipment, Kollo plays an audio sequence of repeating terms — ‘blind spot’, ‘parking spot, ‘piggy bank’ and so on — to examine how the brain represents the transitions between stimuli, and how they are influenced by frequency and familiarity. As the words ring through the theatre, some trigger brain perturbations that sweep across the waveforms representing the probe’s output — a clear sign that it is picking up activity.

Scientists have long conducted experiments during neurosurgery, which offers a rare opportunity to access a living (and often awake) human brain. But Neuropixels probes might provide researchers with the sharpest view of the organ yet.

Since their debut in 2017, Neuropixels have transformed how neuroscientists do electrophysiology experiments in animals, allowing them to record electrical activity from hundreds, sometimes even tens of thousands, of neurons at once. Over the past year, at the NHNN, which is part of the University College London Hospitals, Kollo and his colleagues have been collaborating with neurosurgeons such as Toma to take Neuropixels recordings in people.

Medicine Nobel awarded for brain ‘switch’ that controls neurons with light

Medicine Nobel awarded for brain ‘switch’ that controls neurons with light

There are other ways of surveying single-cell activity in large populations of neurons, such as calcium imaging, which tracks the movement of calcium ions that occurs each time a neuron fires. But these techniques can be too slow to capture the action potentials in certain neurons, or require genetically encoded sensors, limiting their use in some organisms and precluding it in humans.

For people, researchers have relied mostly on devices that sit on the surface of the brain and measure population-level activity, such as high-density electrocorticography. There have also long been tools that can make a relatively small number of recordings at the single-cell level, such as the Utah array — a tiny device studded with miniature needles that penetrate about a millimetre into the brain and that has 96 recording channels.

Pierre Bourdillon, a neurosurgeon at the Adolphe de Rothschild Foundation Hospital in Paris, likens the technological leap for human neuroscience enabled by Neuropixels to the difference between trying to decipher conversations from a single microphone at a busy intersection and listening in on those same discussions using individual microphones attached to the speakers’ collars.

“We’re just starting to get to the level of microphones on individual people,” he says. “For non-human animals, this revolution began about 10–15 years ago. Now we’re just starting to see the first teams using this kind of technology in humans.”

A short walk from the NHNN, at the hospital-turned-research institute known as the Cruciform Building at University College London, neuroscientist Matteo Carandini is applying the most cutting-edge version of Neuropixels technology in organisms with much smaller brains.

His team has been using Neuropixels to record tens of thousands of neurons in mouse brains, sometimes for months at a time. On a sunny Monday afternoon in September, he shows me the set-up for Neuropixels Opto1. This version of the technology, which he has helped to develop, combines electrical recording with optogenetics, a method that allows researchers to switch neurons on and off with light.

Neuroscientists Hayley Bounds (left) and Matteo Carandini examine Neuropixels data.Credit: Matteo Carandini and Hayley Bounds

Carandini was one of the first neuroscientists to use Neuropixels, a device that was designed for research in rodents. The idea began with Tim Harris, a biomedical engineer who arrived at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute’s Janelia Research Campus in Ashburn, Virginia, in 2008 with the task of identifying and developing tools that researchers needed. When he asked his colleagues: ‘What do you want to measure that you can’t?’, he discovered that they were missing probes for conducting long-term, large-scale electrophysiology experiments. In living animals, these involve directly measuring the electrical properties of neurons.

At the time, researchers mostly probed the brain with arrays of twisted four-wire electrodes, which could be combined to record from a few dozen channels at once, or silicon probes, which typically had around 32 recording sites. But they wanted a more comprehensive view of how the cells in the brain work together to perform the organ’s crucial functions — and for that, they would need to collect recordings from many more neurons.

After attempting a few designs on his own, Harris contacted the Interuniversity Microelectronics Centre (Imec), a research institute in Leuven, Belgium, that helped to pioneer some of the world’s most advanced microchips. To Harris’s surprise, Barun Dutta, chief scientist of Imec’s semiconductor technology and systems centre, agreed to take on the task.

How our brains decode speech: special neurons process certain sounds

How our brains decode speech: special neurons process certain sounds

Together, they developed Neuropixels 1.0. The silicon probe comprises 960 recording sites along the hair-thin shank. Each of the recording channels was small enough to capture the action potentials of individual neurons — and 384 of those could be read out in parallel. The shank was attached to a chip the size of a nano SIM card, which holds the electronics required to read, amplify and digitize signals. The outputs could be read with just two wires; this was a major advance at a time when most other devices required each recording channel to have its own wire.

The team reported2 its design in 2017. In that article, Carandini and around three dozen neuroscientists across several laboratories who had tested the device showed that it was possible to insert two of these probes — each weighing about 250 milligrams — into a mouse, allowing them to record around 700 neurons across 5 brain regions at the same time.

Neuropixels 2.0, a smaller, lighter-weight, four-shank probe with 5,120 recording sites (1,536 of which could read out at once), arrived four years later3. (The 1.0 and 2.0 probes are available from Imec for about US$1,700 and $1,800 each, respectively.)

Neuropixels probes have transformed the way neuroscience can be done, says Carandini, who is using the probes to study how the brain processes and uses sensory signals. They enabled the tracking of individual action potentials from thousands of neurons at once and made it possible to record across multiple brain regions in the mouse brain, which is only about one centimetre long.

Using Neuropixels, researchers have found that signals associated with certain sensory, cognitive and motor functions are more widely distributed in the brain than previously thought4. These probes have also enabled scientists to study neural manifolds, the unique patterns of activity that form in populations of brain cells.

Several collaborative efforts known as brain observatories, in which multiple independent teams carry out the same experiments in a standardized manner, have collected vast amounts of Neuropixels data. In one 2025 study5, for example, a dozen labs in the United States and Europe, known as the International Brain Laboratory, came together to collect recordings from more than 620,000 neurons across 279 regions from 139 mice. The result was a brain-wide map of neural activity for both cognitive and motor functions, such as vision, movement and decision-making.

Around 1,700 labs around the world have used Neuropixels in more than two dozen species, including zebra finches, bearded dragons and octopuses. “I was completely taken aback at the variety of species that researchers used these for,” Harris says.

Scientists studying non-human primates were particularly keen: their existing tools either had too few recording channels or could access only the superficial layers of the brain. Harris, Dutta and their colleagues worked with the research community to create Neuropixels 1.0 NHP6, which featured a thicker shank to penetrate the tough membrane around the brain of non-human primates and, at 4 cm in length, could record from deeper structures. (These cost about $4,200 each, according to Dutta.)

Tirin Moore, a neuroscientist at Stanford University in California, who was involved in that effort, says that before Neuropixels, researchers would collect recordings from around two dozen neurons of non-human primates on a good day; now, they routinely record from at least 100. Without these tools, primate neuroscience “would still be in the dark ages”, he says. Moore and his colleagues plan to use the NHP probes to create a high-resolution neural activity map of the visual system of macaque monkeys as part of the Enigma Project, an initiative based at Stanford to record and decode the brain.

A Neuropixels probe records brain activity during surgery to remove part of a person’s brain.Credit: Mihaly Kollo/UCLH

#767. From nightmare debut season to Everton hero - Barry's revival

Last season Thierno Barry scored eight goals in 41 appearances.

This season it's taken him just 12 games to match that tally.

On Monday night Barry scored against Newcastle for the second time in five days as his side earned a deserved win at St James' Park in the Premier League.

Only Erling Haaland (13) has scored more goals among Premier League players in all competitions this season than Barry (eight).

The 24-year-old is on his best run of form since joining the club from Villarreal last summer and, as Everton's only recognised senior striker following Beto's transfer to Fiorentina, is currently indispensable to the Toffees.

By scoring once again Barry highlighted why Everton paid Â£27m for a striker who grew up watching Wayne Rooney and Romelu Lukaku score for the Toffees.

The Frenchman had a rough start to life on Merseyside, having just one shot across his first 16 Everton games, and last month posted a video of himself breaking down during a private training session last season.

That moment was contrasted by his celebration on Monday night, which started with a knee slide and ended with dance moves.

"I was working a lot during the summer and now we can see the result," Barry told Sky Sports.

"The season is long but I'm happy to help the team with my goals.

"I want to enjoy more than last season and I enjoyed my celebration so I am happy."

It was a controversial strike though with Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle telling BBC Sport there was "a clear foul on Fabian Schar" in the build-up.

Who produced the kind of performance Moyes loves? - player ratings

Grealish can still have Everton future - Moyes

Jeers again as home woes continue - Jaissle has big problems at Newcastle

Everton hold off Newcastle United to move in to seventh

In the Premier League Barry leads the way for being involved in the highest proportion of his team's big chances.

Before Monday's match, Everton had recorded 24 big chances, and Barry had been involved in 15 of them (62.5%).

The striker has often been criticised for being wasteful in front of goal.

In Monday's match, for instance, he latched on to Jarrad Branthwaite's flick-on but, when through on goal, made a poor connection with the ball and scuffed his shot.

His goal - a tap-in from two yards - was very difficult not to convert, with the opportunity having had an incredibly high xG of 0.995.

"We know Barry misses chances, but we also know this season he keeps going and he scores goals," former Liverpool and England defender Jamie Carragher told Sky Sports.

His manager David Moyes added: "We're thrilled he's getting the goals because you need your centre-forward to score. He has missed a few but thankfully tonight he was on the spot to get the goal."
